title: Associations between male child marriage and intimate partner violence across low- and middle-income countries
methods: multi-categorical exposure and covariate sensitivity analyses
data_sources: Demographic and Health Surveys (DHS) men's questionnaire and domestic-violence module
UNDP Gender Inequality Index (Human Development Reports)
World Bank country income classification (GNI per capita)
World Bank Women, Business and the Law (1971-2024)
Article Source Data XLSX (Figs. 1-3, Extended Data Tables 1-10)

data_scope.unit_of_analysis: individual men (DHS men's records), pooled across countries
outcomes: IPV victimization by women, including physical IPV
data_scope.exposure: first marriage/union before age 18 (male child marriage)
data_scope.headline_attribution: 17%-25% of IPV cases among men aged 20-24 years
data_scope.sample_size: not stated in the openly accessible text (article is hybrid access; Methods/Results paywalled)
data_scope.survey_years: not stated in the openly accessible text; per-country rosters are in Extended Data Tables 1-2
data_scope.country_roster_note: perpetration and victimization samples cover different country sets (Extended Data Tables 1 and 2 respectively)

core_conclusion: Across 41 LMICs, men who married before age 18 have substantially higher risks of perpetrating nearly all types of intimate partner violence and of experiencing physical IPV in the past 12 months. Counter-intuitively the associations are stronger in lower-gender-inequality or higher-income contexts and attenuated in disadvantaged settings; at country level the GII-IPV correlation holds only among men without a child-marriage history. Male child marriage accounts for an estimated 17%-25% of IPV cases among men aged 20-24.
why_it_matters: Puts boys, not only girls, into the child-marriage evidence base; converts a risk factor into a policy-sized population attributable fraction (17%-25% at ages 20-24); reverses the assumed context gradient by showing the largest effects in less unequal and richer settings; and shows that country-level gender-inequality indices do not translate uniformly into individual risk once early-marriage exposure is accounted for.
why_nature: Global scale with a harmonized instrument (41 LMICs via standardized DHS modules); a counter-intuitive and generalizable pattern rather than a national case study; direct translation into two named policy levers (structural delay of marriage plus targeted support for existing early unions); crosses risk-factor epidemiology, sociology and human behaviour; and fills a genuine measurement gap on an SDG 5.3 population with almost no multi-country evidence.
